Attention amid chaos · 2022

Everything Everywhere All at OnceAttention in the Infinite

Marina considers how Daniels turn multiverse spectacle, elastic editing, and comic excess into an intimate study of attention and care.

By MarinaOctober 17, 20262 min readSpoiler-light review

In this review

A Multiverse Built from Everyday PressureWhen Abundance Becomes Its Own ArgumentSources & references
Film
Everything Everywhere All at Once
Director
Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert
Year
2022

Everything Everywhere All at Once begins with a woman buried under ordinary obligations: taxes, family, translation, the small humiliations of a day that will not hold still. Then the Daniels split that pressure open into a science-fiction adventure, but the film’s real subject is attention. Evelyn Wang is asked to look across impossible distances and notice the people already beside her. I love how the story makes emotional neglect feel less like cruelty than a distracted habit—one that can be changed, though never neatly.

A Multiverse Built from Everyday Pressure

The film’s greatest pleasure is its collision of registers. A fluorescent government office, a kung-fu brawl, a cramped family argument, and an absurd visual gag can occupy the same breath without cancelling one another out. Its editing moves like a mind scrolling too fast, while Son Lux’s score gives the rush a pulse that is both anxious and tender. Michelle Yeoh anchors this turbulence with extraordinary physical and emotional precision; she can make a gesture look brave, ridiculous, or heartbreaking before the scene has finished changing shape.

I am especially moved by the way the film treats alternate lives not simply as spectacle, but as a grammar for regret. Each possibility carries the faint pressure of a question: what might I have become if I had chosen differently, or listened sooner? The multiverse lets the movie speak about immigrant dislocation and generational distance without turning either into a lesson. Its wildest images keep circling back to a modest wish—to be understood by someone who has learned to see you differently.

The performances make that wish persuasive. Stephanie Hsu gives Joy a volatile brightness that can turn from comic excess to exposed feeling in an instant, while Ke Huy Quan finds surprising force in gentleness. James Hong and Jamie Lee Curtis sharpen the film’s crowded social world, where affection often arrives disguised as irritation. Even the physical comedy has character in it: bodies become signs of frustration, longing, and the strange ways people ask for care when direct language fails.

When Abundance Becomes Its Own Argument

Still, the film’s abundance is also its limitation. The barrage of jokes, references, costumes, universes, and tonal pivots can flatten its own emotional emphasis; sometimes a feeling is introduced, underlined, and underlined again before the next invention arrives. The screenplay occasionally mistakes accumulation for escalation. Yet that excess is not incidental. It recreates the exhaustion it describes, the sense of living amid too many tabs open at once. I sometimes wanted the film to pause, but its refusal to settle is part of its argument.

What stays with me is not the question of which universe matters most, but the film’s insistence that meaning is made through repeated, imperfect acts of care. The Daniels build a maximalist machine and then point it toward a very intimate scale: a hand offered, a sentence reconsidered, a person given another chance to be heard. Everything Everywhere All at Once is noisy, sentimental, and occasionally overstuffed. It is also unusually sincere about how attention can become a form of love.
